definition: A violent, unruly troublemaker, especially one involved in gang or crowd violence.
origin: Hooligan is widely believed to derive from Hooligan, the surname of a rowdy, possibly fictional Irish family, or a specific unruly individual, in 1890s London, popularised through a music hall song and newspaper crime reports about their disorderly, often drunken behaviour. The name spread rapidly through the press to describe any violent street rowdy, well before its later, specific association with football crowd violence.

definition: Describing a map projection that represents lines of constant compass direction as straight lines, widely used for navigation.
origin: Mercator projection is named after Gerardus Mercator (1512–1594), the Flemish cartographer who in 1569 devised a way to project the curved surface of the globe onto a flat rectangle so that any straight line drawn on the map corresponded to a constant compass bearing, an enormous aid to sailors. The projection's well-known drawback, distorting the size of regions far from the equator, still bears his name today.

definition: Relating to the Marxist theories of Leon Trotsky, especially permanent worldwide revolution rather than socialism in a single nation.
origin: Trotskyist is named after Leon Trotsky (1879–1940), a leading figure of the Russian Revolution alongside Lenin, who after Stalin rose to power argued for "permanent revolution" spreading communism worldwide, rather than Stalin's policy of building "socialism in one country" first. Exiled and eventually assassinated by a Stalinist agent in Mexico with an ice axe, Trotsky's name lived on as shorthand for this rival, internationalist strand of Marxism.

definition: An imaginary evil figure used to frighten children, or a person or thing that is a source of fear or blame.
origin: Bogeyman most likely traces to "bogey" or "bogle," old English and Scots words for a goblin or spectre, themselves possibly connected to "Boggart," a household spirit of English and Welsh folklore, or even distantly to Bonaparte, whom some claim was invoked to frighten British children with the threat of "Boney" coming to get them. The exact ancestor is disputed, but the word settled into a generic name for any invented figure of dread used to enforce obedience or explain misfortune.

definition: Relating to the legal requirement that a person be informed of their rights to silence and legal counsel upon arrest.
origin: Miranda rights are named after Ernesto Miranda, a man arrested in Phoenix, Arizona in 1963 and convicted based on a confession he gave without being told he had the right to remain silent or to a lawyer. His case reached the US Supreme Court, which ruled in 1966 that such warnings must be given before any police interrogation, and "reading someone their Miranda rights" has been standard procedure ever since.
